content: 1. Cefadroxil can be administered orally at a dose of 1 gram daily, either as a single dose or divided into two doses every 12 hours, for a duration of 10 days. Alternatively, a dose of 2 grams daily can be used, either as a single dose or divided every 12 hours. 2. For prophylaxis in dental or upper respiratory procedures, administer 2 grams of cefadroxil orally one hour before the procedure. 3. In cases of renal impairment, the dosing interval of cefadroxil should be adjusted based on creatinine clearance (CrCl): CrCl 25–50 mL/min: Administer every 12 hours. CrCl 10–25 mL/min: Administer once daily. CrCl <10 mL/min: Administer every 36 hours. 4. Cefadroxil is effective against organisms such as E. coli, Proteus mirabilis, Klebsiella species, staphylococci, and group A beta-hemolytic streptococci. 5. For pediatric prophylaxis in dental or upper respiratory procedures, administer 50 mg/kg orally one hour before the procedure, not exceeding 2 grams. 6. For pediatric infections, administer 30 mg/kg/day orally, either as a single dose or divided every 12 hours, for 10 days. The maximum dose should not exceed 1 gram per dose. 7. Cefadroxil reduces the efficacy of live bacterial vaccines, such as the BCG vaccine, due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Live bacterial vaccines should not be administered until the antibiotic course is completed. 8. Cefadroxil decreases the efficacy of the cholera vaccine. Avoid coadministration with systemic antibiotics, as they may act against the vaccine strain. Do not administer the cholera vaccine to patients who have received antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. 9. Cefadroxil may reduce the effectiveness of oral microbiota products containing bacterial spores. Complete the antibiotic regimen 2–4 days before initiating microbiota therapy. 10. Cefadroxil reduces the efficacy of the live typhoid vaccine. Administration of live bacterial vaccines should be delayed until the antibiotic course is completed. 11. Cefadroxil may increase the nephrotoxic and/or ototoxic effects of aminoglycosides such as amikacin, gentamicin, kanamycin, neomycin, streptomycin, and tobramycin. Use caution and monitor renal function closely. 12. Cefadroxil may interfere with the therapeutic effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors, such as atezolizumab, avelumab, balstilimab, cemiplimab, dostarlimab, durvalumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, penpulimab, sintilimab, and toripalimab. Use caution and monitor closely. 13. Cefadroxil may alter intestinal flora, reducing the effectiveness of oral hormonal contraceptives, including estradiol, conjugated estrogens, ethinyl estradiol, and mestranol. Although the risk of contraceptive failure is low, caution and monitoring are advised. 14. Cefadroxil may increase the levels or effects of acidic (anionic) drugs, such as aspirin, diclofenac, ibuprofen, indomethacin, ketoprofen, naproxen, and others, by competing for renal tubular clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is generally minor or unknown. 15. Cefadroxil may increase the levels or effects of certain diuretics, such as hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, and metolazone, through competition for renal tubular clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is minor or unknown. 16. Cefadroxil may increase the levels or effects of drugs like digoxin and ganciclovir by altering intestinal flora or competing for renal clearance. Use caution and monitor closely. 17. Cefadroxil may increase the risk of nephrotoxicity when coadministered with drugs associated with nephrotoxic effects, such as voclosporin and furosemide. Monitor renal function closely. 18. Cefadroxil may increase the effects of anticoagulants like warfarin through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Use caution and monitor coagulation parameters. 19. Cefadroxil may reduce the levels or effects of certain vitamins, such as biotin, thiamine, pantothenic acid, and pyridoxine, by altering intestinal flora. This applies only to oral forms of these agents, and the clinical significance is generally minor or unknown. 20. Cefadroxil may increase the levels or effects of NSAIDs, such as celecoxib, etodolac, fenoprofen, flurbiprofen, and others, through competition for renal tubular clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is minor or unknown. 21. Cefadroxil may increase the levels or effects of certain antibiotics, such as aztreonam, through pharmacodynamic synergy. This combination may be used synergistically against Enterobacteriaceae. 22.
